cards.title: Map the five link-building types to an ecommerce backlink mix
cards.summary: Foundational, guest post, niche edit, expert-quote, linkable-asset and digital-PR links each play a different role in a Shopify store's off-page profile.
cards.use_when: Planning a quarterly off-page SEO plan for a store and deciding where to spend outreach time and budget.
steps: Treat foundational links (social profiles, business/citation directories, Web 2.0 sites) as the base layer that signals your site exists and what it is about; the source says these are mostly free and Google-endorsed, so build them first before anything else.

Make guest posts and niche edits the 'bread and butter' for ecommerce: guest posts let you control content, anchor text and the target URL, so you can point a link from an interior-design blog to a specific curtain collection page. Niche edits add your link to an already-published, already-trafficked article, which the source argues is faster and often more powerful because existing pages pass link equity immediately.

Use expert-quote platforms (the source calls it HARO, now rebranded Connectively — verify the current name/interface) to answer journalist queries in your category, e.g. advice on choosing curtains for bright rooms, and earn editorial links when quoted.
Build linkable assets (comprehensive guides, infographics, calculators) on your own site, then do light outreach to relevant sites telling them the asset exists and asking for a link.
Use digital PR — a data-driven insight or press release pitched to journalists and bloggers — when you want the highest-quality editorial links.

Decide per link whether to target the domain or a collection/product page: the source recommends 50–75% of links to the main domain in the first ~3 months, with the rest on low-hanging-fruit collection pages.
caveats: The 50–75% domain-share rule is the source's rule of thumb for the first three months, to be adjusted afterward based on competition and results.
Tool names (Semrush, Ahrefs, HARO/Connectively, Snov.io, Hunter) change interfaces and pricing — verify current functionality.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.

cards.title: Judge a backlink's quality before pursuing it
cards.summary: Six factors — follow status, anchor text, topical relevance, authority metrics, link target page and site quality — determine whether a backlink helps or hurts your store.
cards.use_when: Vetting a prospect site or an inbound link offer before you write a guest post, accept a placement or pay a fee.
steps: Check dofollow vs nofollow: dofollow links pass value; nofollow passes little. The source says a natural mix is fine, but focus effort on dofollow links.

Review anchor text: the visible clickable text should be descriptive and relevant, e.g. 'office chairs' for an office-chair page, so search engines receive the right topical signal. Keep it natural — over-optimized anchor patterns stand out against competitors.

Assess page-level relevance and site-level relevance: the article should relate to the page it links to, and the host site should sit in or near your industry (an interior-design site is a good fit for a curtain brand).
Check authority metrics (Moz Domain Authority, Ahrefs Domain Rating): aim higher, but treat them as manipulable — read them alongside the other factors rather than as the sole test.

Consider the linked page: send links to the page you actually want to rank, such as a collection page, but don't wildly exceed competitor link counts — if competitors have ~10 links to a page, building 30 'sticks out like a sore thumb' and risks penalties.
Prefer a few high-quality links over many low-quality ones.
caveats: Authority metrics can be gamed; the source explicitly says to interpret them in context, not in isolation.
The source presents over-building relative to competitors as a penalty risk; this is the presenter's framing, not a stated Google threshold.

cards.title: Run a link-gap analysis and set a monthly link target
cards.summary: Compare your filtered dofollow referring-domain count against SEO competitors to derive a concrete monthly backlink goal.
cards.use_when: Setting link-building targets for a store and deciding how many placements per month to buy or earn.
steps: In Semrush or Ahrefs, filter your backlinks to dofollow only and to referring domains with DR/DA of at least 30 (the source's chosen floor). Count the result — e.g. 105 referring domains.
Apply the identical filters to your SEO competitors' profiles; the source analyzed three or more and averaged around 203 referring domains in its example.
Subtract your count from the competitor average (203 − 105 = ~98 referring domains needed) to size the gap.
Convert the gap into a cadence: spreading 98 links over 24 months is about 4 new links per month, but the source recommends aiming for roughly 6–8 per month to keep pace as competitors also build.
Re-run the link-gap analysis periodically to confirm you are still competitive.
caveats: The 105/203/98 figures are an illustrative example, not a benchmark for any particular niche.
The DR/DA 30 filter is a source-specific heuristic; adjust the floor upward if your own profile is stronger.

cards.title: Screen spam links with a five-point checklist
cards.summary: Before accepting or paying for a placement, verify the site is real, topically relevant, has organic traffic and has quality backlinks of its own.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a paid link offer, an inbound guest-post pitch or an email offering backlinks for a store.
steps: Check it is a real site people care about: open it, judge design and content quality, and see whether it writes about one industry or about everything — general 'we cover anything' blogs are often link-selling sites to avoid.
Check history with the Wayback Machine: if the domain previously covered a different topic (the source's example: a former casino site now presenting as interior design), treat that as a red flag.
Check niche relevance: the site should discuss what your brand is about. Avoid general blogs built solely to sell links.
Check organic traffic: look for real traffic that is trending upward or at least stable. The source's bare minimum is 1,000 visitors per month, and sudden traffic dips can signal a penalty.
Check the site's own backlink quality: if the host site's inbound links are poor, it passes poor link equity to you.
Avoid bought links from cheap marketplaces (the source cites Fiverr and unsolicited backlink emails) — low quality at best, ranking damage at worst.
caveats: The 1,000-visitors-per-month minimum is the source's stated bare minimum, not an industry standard.
The source notes you can double-check cheap links because some may be fine, but says they usually are not.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.

cards.title: Build foundational links and citations as the base layer
cards.summary: Set up social profiles, directory listings and Web 2.0 pages so search engines can identify your store as a real entity before you pursue editorial links.
cards.use_when: Launching a new store or a new brand with no backlink profile, before starting guest posting or outreach.
steps: Build foundational links — social profiles, business directory and local citations, plus Web 2.0 pages such as Medium or Behance. The source frames this as 'entity stacking': helping Google understand who you are so it can rank you.
Do not just create the profile and drop your URL in the about page: fill in the full business information and post some content and images so the listing sends strong identity signals.

For citations, prepare a standard data set: business name, owner name, address, city, telephone, website URL, business description, target keywords (e.g. shopping-page keywords) and logo. The source says you likely already have this and AI can help draft descriptions.
Target at least 30 foundational links — the source's own internal target, described as safe and free, though fewer may suffice.
Consider outsourcing citation building, as the source does, because doing it manually takes a lot of time.
caveats: The 30-link target is the source's internal goal, not a calculated requirement.
Vanity or incomplete profiles add little; the value is in filled-out, active listings.

cards.title: Prioritize low-hanging-fruit collection pages for links
cards.summary: Use Semrush's organic research to find pages ranking in positions 4–10, then send links there because they are closest to converting rankings into revenue.
cards.use_when: Choosing which collection or category pages to build links to this month on a store.
steps: Open Semrush's Organic Research tool for your domain and filter positions to 4–10.
The output is the set of your pages sitting on page one but not yet in the top three — the source's 'low-hanging fruit' that can be pushed into the top three fastest.
Pick roughly three to five of these pages per month depending on your link-building budget, and save them as your monthly link targets alongside the main domain.
Balance this against the source's 50–75% domain-share rule for the first three months: juice the root domain while also pushing the easiest collection pages.
Rebalance toward collection pages after a few months based on competition and observed results.
caveats: The instruction is written for Semrush but the source says it is translatable to Ahrefs.
The 3–5 pages and 50–75% domain split are rules of thumb, explicitly dependent on brand age and existing link profile.

cards.title: Prospect link targets by scraping competitors' guest-post backlinks
cards.summary: Identify true SEO competitors, scrape their placement-type backlinks in Semrush, then filter the export to reachable, healthy, relevant sites.
cards.use_when: Building an outreach prospect list for a store's guest posting and niche edit campaign.
steps: Determine SEO competition — the brands winning the SERPs for your target keywords, which may differ from your brand competitors. Use Semrush's Keyword Overview to read the SERP for a key term such as 'sheer curtains'.

Pick mid-sized niche competitors rather than giants: the source excluded Target, Walmart and Ikea because scraping their backlinks yields mostly unreachable or irrelevant prospects. Collect at least five SEO competitor domains.

In Semrush Backlink Analytics, open the Backlinks tab for a competitor and filter to: dofollow links, one link per referring domain, 'content' placement (so the link sits inside article content, implying a guest post), and platform = blog. Export the results.

Run the exported domains through Semrush's Bulk Analysis tool set to root domain, then filter to sites with monthly visits greater than 1,000 and an authority score of 15 or above (raise the threshold if your own profile is stronger).
Repeat for the other SEO competitors to build a refined prospect list.
If the list is thin, expand prospecting beyond SEO competitors to any site in your niche, or in adjacent niches (for curtain brands: interior design, home improvement, family/mom blogs).
caveats: The 1,000 visits and authority-score 15 thresholds are the source's heuristics.
Stay natural: the source warns against clearly irrelevant placements, e.g. an outdoor blog linking to a curtain brand.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.

cards.title: Find contact details for link prospects
cards.summary: Use email-finding tools for speed, or fall back to manual site inspection, personal emails and contact forms.
cards.use_when: Turning a filtered prospect list into a sendable outreach list for guest posts or niche edits.
steps: Use a paid email-finding tool as the primary route — the source recommends Snov.io based on its results and clean lists, and notes Hunter.io as another option used by some SEOs; verify current pricing and data coverage.

If not paying for tools, go site by site into the contact page and look for a named person's email (chris@domain.com) rather than a generic inbox (info@domain.com), because a real person is less likely to bin the message.
Check the about page for owner names, then find their social profiles and reach out there.
Use site contact forms: the source says these almost always reach the site owner, and a well-crafted message can get a reply.
Send direct messages on social platforms referencing their site and asking whether they accept guest posts.
caveats: Manual research takes far more time and may not yield a usable contact, which is why the source prefers paid tools.
Tool names and capabilities change; confirm the current product before subscribing.

Editorial qualification: paid placements must use rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow"; do not buy unqualified links to manipulate rankings. Assess sponsored placements by relevant referral traffic and commercial value, not promised ranking credit.

cards.title: Write outreach subject lines and bodies that get opened and answered
cards.summary: Personalize subject lines with curiosity, humor or a question, and keep the body short, specific and clear about wanting a dofollow guest post.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first outreach email to a blog or site owner to request a guest post placement.
steps: Make the subject line both highly relevant and attention-grabbing — the source says if it only grabs attention without relevance, it reads as spam. Include the recipient's name and their domain, e.g. 'Quick question, Chris, about curtains.com'.
Use curiosity: a question about their own site works because it piques the owner's interest.
Use humor where it fits your niche — the source says jokes in the subject plus a matching answer in the body have worked well for them, and suggests testing combinations of tactics in your own niche.
In the body, state your intention to write content for their site and the type of content you specialize in, and make clear a dofollow link is desired.
Say explicitly that you are willing to pay any publishing fee if required — the source says you will most likely pay for these links.
Keep it short and to the point, and customize the free template rather than sending it verbatim: the source argues generic templates underperform because everyone has the same one.
caveats: The source states Google does not officially support buying links and may treat manipulative links as link spam, while asserting that paid links are widely used and work when done properly — treat this as the source's position, not a safe harbor.
The claim that a well-crafted message beats ~70% of template users is the source's assertion, not a measured benchmark.
